newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Romanian unions claim wage victory, IMF watches.
newsitem.headline: Romanian unions claim wage victory, IMF watches.

text.p: Romania's big trade unions claimed victory in talks with the government on Tuesday, securing pay concessions, wage indexation and continued electricity price subsidies.
The agreement followed a resumption of negotiations, broken off last week when the unions walked out of a session with Prime Minister Victor Ciorbea.

It coincided with lengthy cabinet discussions on revising the 1997 budget and winning the approval of a visiting International Monetary Fund mission to pay out the second of five $86 million disbursements to underpin market reforms.
Ministers of the centrist coalition, seen bickering publicly over budget allocations in the past week, proceeded with discussions on Tuesday evening.

"We agreed on a 17 percent wage indexation for the third quarter of 1997 and six percent for the fourth quarter," Dumitru Costin, leader of the National Trade Union (BNSD) bloc, told reporters at the end of talks.
"This indexation should be combined with tax cuts and should lead to an increase in real wages of 16 percent until the end of the year."
He said the IMF had endorsed the accord, including a provision to continue subsidising electricity prices to help Romanians through the 1997-1998 winter.
No government minister was available to comment on the outcome of the talks.

The IMF is expected to say on Wednesday whether it backs the revised budget and to pass judgement on progress in curbing inflation, proceeding with stalled privatisation and closing down inefficient farms and companies.

Newspaper reports said the Fund had objected to government proposals to extend the limit on external borrowing and had pointed to shortcomings in industrial restructuring and passing market-oriented legislation.

Since the centrists defeated ex-communists in last year's election, they have pledged to make up for seven years of stalling which left Romania's economic reforms trailing far behind those of Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic.

Monthly inflation, which soared to more than 30 percent in March after price liberalisation, is expected to fall below two percent this month, though the government's original target of 90 percent for the year has long since passed out of reach.
Ministers have pledged to stick to their original target of reducing the budget deficit to 4.5 percent of Gross Domestic Product from last year's 5.8 percent.
